intro.title: Atlantic County
intro.summary: Atlantic County stretches from Atlantic City's barrier-island shoreline through mainland suburbs, small inland cities, and Pinelands communities. Its real estate includes oceanfront and bayfront condominiums, older city neighborhoods, suburban single-family homes, and properties with more land farther inland. The Atlantic City Expressway, Garden State Parkway, U.S. Route 30, NJ Transit rail service, and Atlantic City International Airport connect different parts of the county. Beaches, marinas, golf courses, wineries, county parks, Stockton University, and Atlantic City's entertainment district all contribute to the county's unusually varied character.

communities.title: Absecon
communities.summary: Absecon's waterways connect its early shellfishing settlement with the story of the shore beyond it. Clamming and oystering supported the first settlers, while local physician Jonathan Pitney later helped turn his vision for an Absecon Island resort into the railroad connection that brought Atlantic City into being.

sources.title: Atlantic County: Absecon and Absecon Island history

communities.title: Atlantic City
communities.summary: Atlantic City's street plan carries its seaside origins in plain sight: avenues parallel to the ocean take the names of bodies of water, and cross streets take the names of states. The railroad's arrival in 1854 helped transform the island settlement into a resort, followed by its first Boardwalk in 1870.

sources.title: City of Atlantic City: history and original street plan
Atlantic County: Absecon Island and Atlantic City history

communities.title: Brigantine
communities.summary: Ocean beach and the Absecon estuary frame opposite sides of Brigantine, giving the barrier island distinct oceanfront and bayside edges. Its sole road connection crosses the inlet toward Atlantic City; the present bridge follows an earlier crossing destroyed by the hurricane of 1944.

sources.title: City of Brigantine: Floodplain Management Plan, island geography and bridge history

communities.title: Buena Borough
communities.summary: Buena Borough brings together three older settlements: Buena, Landisville and Minotola. Their separate post offices, established in the late nineteenth century, help explain why these place names retain their own identities within a borough formed much later.

sources.title: Borough of Buena: history, settlement names and historic photographs

communities.title: Buena Vista Township
communities.summary: Farmland around Richland, East Vineland and Milmay gives Buena Vista Township much of its inland character. Collings Lakes has a different origin: cranberry bogs were transformed into lakes for a residential community in the 1950s, adding a lake-centered settlement to the township's older agricultural villages.

sources.title: Buena Vista Township: community geography and settlement history

communities.title: Corbin City
communities.summary: The Tuckahoe River is central to Corbin City's setting and to the working history it shares with neighboring Tuckahoe. In the nineteenth century, this stretch of river supported bog-iron production, window-glass manufacturing and schooners sailing between the villages and the sea.

sources.title: City of Corbin City: historical notes on the Tuckahoe River villages
City of Corbin City: riverside community overview

communities.title: Egg Harbor City
communities.summary: Egg Harbor City's central park and surviving public squares trace a town planned before the Civil War. Its founders imagined a port on the Mullica River, but the railroad drew the center south, where the city developed as a commercial hub for the surrounding farming country.

sources.title: Atlantic County: Egg Harbor City's original plan and surviving squares
City of Egg Harbor: river-port plan and railroad development

communities.title: Egg Harbor Township
communities.summary: Egg Harbor Township's modern suburban landscape has roots in a much larger coastal township from which several shore communities separated. Along the Great Egg Harbor River, its earlier economy depended on shipbuilding, oystering and timber, a maritime history that sits behind the mainland's later residential growth.

sources.title: Egg Harbor Township: history of the original township and river economy

communities.title: Estell Manor
communities.summary: Forest now covers ground in Estell Manor that once supported glassmaking and wartime industry. Within the county park, the Estellville Glassworks ruins preserve the footprint of a nineteenth-century factory, with foundations and furnace remains connecting the wooded landscape to its industrial past.

sources.title: Atlantic County: Estell Manor Park landscape and industrial history
Atlantic County: Estellville Glassworks historic site

communities.title: Folsom
communities.summary: Folsom's neighborhoods sit within a broader Pinelands landscape of forest, wetlands and farmland. Development is concentrated around Folsom Village, Collings Lake and Penny Pot, while streams and man-made lakes along the Hospitality Branch help shape the spaces between those settled areas.

sources.title: Borough of Folsom: Master Plan Reexamination, community form and land cover

communities.title: Galloway Township
communities.summary: Galloway stretches from eastern marshes toward the Pinelands, with several village centers rather than one continuous downtown. Historic Smithville and the crossroads community of Oceanville retain distinct identities, while the township's civic center serves the neighborhoods between the wooded inland area and the coastal refuge landscape.

sources.title: Galloway Township: Municipal Self-Assessment Report, landscape and village cores

communities.title: Hamilton Township (Mays Landing)
communities.summary: Mays Landing gives Hamilton Township a historic center where Main Street and older residential blocks meet the Great Egg Harbor River. The river supported shipping and a cotton mill, while the village's selection as Atlantic County's seat in 1837 added the courthouse to its townscape.

sources.title: National Park Service: Mays Landing Historic District nomination
Atlantic County: county formation and the Mays Landing courthouse

communities.title: Hammonton
communities.summary: Hammonton's downtown gathers around Bellevue Avenue, with residential streets close to its business core and agricultural land beyond it. Hammonton Lake connects that present-day town to its beginnings: an early nineteenth-century sawmill there was followed by glassmaking and the sale of surrounding land to farmers.

sources.title: Town of Hammonton: 2025 Housing Element, downtown and agricultural setting
Atlantic County: Hammonton's lake, sawmill and farming settlement

communities.title: Linwood
communities.summary: Along Shore Road, Linwood's historic district preserves the outline of the earlier settlement of Leedsville. Former sea captains' houses, Victorian homes and early twentieth-century bungalows give these blocks their varied scale, reflecting a community shaped by both maritime work and later railroad and trolley growth.

sources.title: National Park Service: Linwood Historic District nomination

communities.title: Longport
communities.summary: At the southern tip of Absecon Island, Longport sits between the Atlantic Ocean and the bay. Its street numbers preserve an unusual piece of shoreline history: erosion carried away the borough's first ten avenues in the early twentieth century, leaving 11th Avenue as its starting point.

sources.title: Borough of Longport: island geography and the lost avenues

communities.title: Margate City
communities.summary: On Absecon Island, Margate's seaside streets have an unmistakable landmark in Lucy the Elephant, built in 1881. The community was once called South Atlantic City; its historical museum occupies the old City Hall, where exhibits trace the town's development as a home and resort.

sources.title: Margate Public Library: Margate Historical Museum and city history

communities.title: Mullica Township
communities.summary: Old village names and surviving eighteenth-century buildings give Mullica Township a history spread across several settlements. Pleasant Mills hosted the meeting that created the township in 1838; in Nesco, the former Hilda Frame School houses the historical museum.

sources.title: Mullica Township: historical society, villages and schoolhouse museum

communities.title: Northfield
communities.summary: Northfield's Birch Grove landscape has an industrial past: the park occupies the former grounds of local brick companies. Nearby, the joined Casto House and former city library hold the municipal museum, bringing a nineteenth-century home and a reused civic building into one place for the city's history.

sources.title: City of Northfield: Casto House, municipal museum and Birch Grove's brickyard history
City of Northfield: Cultural Committee and museum buildings

communities.title: Pleasantville
communities.summary: Pleasantville's Main Street grew from the meeting of older mainland settlements and the transportation lines that connected them. Railroads helped draw the separate hamlets together, and the early twentieth-century trolley reinforced Main Street as a commercial spine, leaving a town center shaped by successive ways of reaching the shore.

sources.title: City of Pleasantville: Master Plan historic preservation element

communities.title: Port Republic
communities.summary: Nacote Creek and its millpond form the center of Port Republic's old village, with streets bending toward the creek crossings. Nineteenth-century houses line the historic district, recalling a settlement where sawmills, shipyards and coastal trade once concentrated around the water near the Mullica River's mouth.

sources.title: National Park Service: Port Republic Historic District nomination

communities.title: Somers Point
communities.summary: Somers Point's bayfront history is visible in the brick Somers Mansion above Great Egg Harbor Bay. Built in the early 1720s, the house connects the present waterfront to the Somers family and the ferry crossing established there in the late seventeenth century.

sources.title: New Jersey State Park Service: Somers Mansion and ferry history

communities.title: Ventnor City
communities.summary: Ventnor occupies a stretch of Absecon Island between the ocean and the back-bay thoroughfare, with a residential Boardwalk continuing toward Atlantic City. Its name came from the English seaside town of Ventnor in 1889, tying the island community's identity to the resort era in which it developed.

sources.title: City of Ventnor: island setting and naming history
City of Ventnor: Boardwalk and community setting

communities.title: Weymouth Township
communities.summary: Dorothy and Belcoville give Weymouth Township two village centers with different beginnings. Dorothy grew around the railroad in the late nineteenth century, while Belcoville's surviving houses recall a company village built for the Bethlehem Loading Company's workers during World War I.

sources.title: Weymouth Township: Dorothy, Belcoville and the Bethlehem Loading Company

intro.title: Burlington County
intro.summary: Burlington County reaches from Delaware River communities and established suburbs into farmland, forests, and the Pinelands. Housing ranges from historic rowhouses and older borough homes to townhouses, postwar neighborhoods, newer subdivisions, and properties on larger wooded or agricultural lots. I-295, the New Jersey Turnpike, Routes 38, 70, 73, and 130, and NJ Transit's River Line shape travel through the more developed western side of the county. Historic town centers, the Rancocas Creek, Smithville Park, county farm and parkland, and access to the Pine Barrens give the county both metropolitan connections and substantial open space.

communities.title: Bass River Township
communities.summary: New Gretna gives Bass River Township a village center within a much larger Pine Barrens landscape of forest, wetlands, and rivers. The village's history reaches back to the 1700s, when it served as a stagecoach stop for the region's iron mills.

sources.title: Bass River Township 2022 Master Plan Reexamination

communities.title: Beverly City
communities.summary: Beverly's Delaware River setting goes back to its beginnings as the ferry port of Dunks Ferry. A small downtown and riverbank location still give the city a recognizable center, with a history rooted in the water crossing that preceded its nineteenth-century incorporation.

communities.title: Bordentown City
communities.summary: Bordentown's older streets occupy the bluffs above the Delaware River, where the settlement first took shape as Farnsworth's Landing. Its historic district contains buildings from successive generations, with surviving eighteenth-century architecture among the later houses and public buildings.

sources.title: Bordentown City Historic Landmark Overlay District

communities.title: Bordentown Township
communities.summary: Blacks Creek carries part of Bordentown Township's industrial history through the place still known as Dunns Mill. A mill operated here from the early 1700s until a 1901 fire; the creek and former clay-working areas help explain the township's older landscape of milling and brickmaking.

communities.title: Burlington City
communities.summary: High Street leads through Burlington to the Delaware River, where the riverfront promenade opens out along the water. The city's roots reach back to a Quaker settlement established in 1677, giving this river town a colonial history behind its present streets and waterfront.

sources.title: City of Burlington: Learn About Burlington

communities.title: Burlington Township
communities.summary: Burlington Township's Delaware River frontage connects it with a settlement history older than its present neighborhoods. A Dutch settler's riverside log cabin and tavern appeared in the 1660s, followed by Quaker settlement, while river shipping helped shape the community's early development.

communities.title: Chesterfield Township
communities.summary: Chesterfield's older settlements include Crosswicks, Sykesville, and the crossroads village once called Recklesstown. In Chesterfield village itself, the historic district gathers clapboard houses and churches around intersecting village roads, with the old Chesterfield House standing at the central crossroads.

sources.title: National Park Service: Village of Chesterfield Historic District

communities.title: Cinnaminson Township
communities.summary: Cinnaminson's older landmarks carry several strands of local history into the present. The former Phillips School, built for Black pupils in the nineteenth century, now houses the Footlighters theater, while Westfield Friends Meeting reflects the area's much earlier Quaker roots.

communities.title: Delanco Township
communities.summary: Delanco takes its name from the two waters that meet here: the Delaware River and Rancocas Creek. The settlement grew from the older Wilmerton property beside the creek, with steamboat landings and a nineteenth-century railroad station helping turn riverbank land into a village.

communities.title: Delran Township
communities.summary: The Delaware River and Rancocas Creek give Delran both its name and the edges of its distinctive L-shaped geography. Older places such as Bridgeboro and the mill settlement on Swedes Run add a village and water-powered industrial past to the township's present landscape.

communities.title: Eastampton Township
communities.summary: Historic Smithville gives Eastampton a visible nineteenth-century village, with restored workers' houses and an 1840 Greek Revival mansion. This was the industrial home of Hezekiah Smith, whose machinery business also made high-wheel bicycles, leaving a factory-village history within today's county-owned grounds.

sources.title: Burlington County: Historic Smithville Park and Village

communities.title: Edgewater Park Township
communities.summary: Edgewater Park's landscape combines an older Delaware River settlement at Riverbank with neighborhoods largely developed after World War II. The river-facing section around Warren and Woodlane avenues preserves an earlier layer of a township whose residential growth came much later than its agricultural beginnings.

sources.title: Edgewater Park Township Land Use Plan

communities.title: Evesham Township (Marlton)
communities.summary: Olde Marlton Village gives Evesham an older center whose buildings recall its nineteenth-century growth. Marlton's name comes from marl, the clay-like material once dug locally for fertilizer; that industry helped expand a village whose origins preceded the township's later suburban development.

communities.title: Fieldsboro Borough
communities.summary: White Hill Mansion overlooks the Delaware River in Fieldsboro, tying the borough's name to the Fields family who occupied it for generations. Its brick Georgian core and later shingled additions make the house a visible record of several periods in this riverfront settlement's history.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: White Hill Mansion

communities.title: Florence Township
communities.summary: Florence and Roebling give the township two distinct Delaware River industrial-village histories. Florence was laid out with a riverfront residential street and a commercial center farther inland, while Roebling's brick workers' houses grew around the steel-wire plant that helped supply major suspension bridges.

communities.title: Hainesport Township
communities.summary: Hainesport sits between the north and south branches of Rancocas Creek, a setting that shaped its early working life. Once known as Herring Hall for its fishery, the settlement later took its name from Barclay Haines and the steamboat port he established along the creek.

communities.title: Lumberton Township
communities.summary: Lumberton's name recalls the timber once floated down Rancocas Creek toward Philadelphia. Earlier mill settlements at Eayrestown and Fostertown add to that water-powered history, while the surviving Ridgway Gaun House on Main Street now serves as a community center and local history museum.

communities.title: Mansfield Township
communities.summary: Columbus, Hedding, and Georgetown give Mansfield separate village centers within a broader agricultural landscape. Older schoolhouses help mark those settlements, including Georgetown's nineteenth-century building and Hedding's brick school, reminders of the local institutions that once served the surrounding farming community.

sources.title: Mansfield Township School District: Historical Columbus

communities.title: Maple Shade Township
communities.summary: Maple Shade grew around a railroad village, with the station's name eventually becoming the township's own. Its early twentieth-century Barlow bungalows and the much older Chesterford Schoolhouse reflect different stages of that growth, from a rural community to the streets of houses that followed.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: Chesterford Schoolhouse

communities.title: Medford Township
communities.summary: Medford Village's brick sidewalks, gas lamps, and Victorian houses give the township a recognizable historic center. Beyond that Main Street setting, Kirby's Mill preserves another part of the local story: a sawmill and gristmill that continued using water power into the twentieth century.

communities.title: Medford Lakes Borough
communities.summary: Lakes, pines, and log houses are central to Medford Lakes' identity. The community began as a 1920s resort built around that wooded waterside setting, and its cedar-log architecture remained part of the borough as seasonal cabins gave way to a year-round town.

communities.title: Moorestown Township
communities.summary: Moorestown's tree-lined Main Street brings historic homes, churches, and the Community House into one downtown streetscape. The center grew along the old King's Highway around Thomas Moore's early eighteenth-century inn, connecting the present town center with the village that gave Moorestown its name.

communities.title: Mount Holly Township
communities.summary: Mount Holly's old mill race still traces a waterway through its historic district, a physical reminder of the industries that helped build the town. The former county prison and the Lyceum add civic landmarks to a place where working waterways and public buildings shaped the center.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: Mount Holly Mill Race Way

communities.title: Mount Laurel Township
communities.summary: Mount Laurel's suburban neighborhoods grew around older farming villages such as Fellowship, Masonville and Centerton. At Paulsdale, the Greek Revival farmhouse where suffragist Alice Paul grew up preserves part of that agricultural landscape, linking the township's rural past with the campaign for women's voting rights.

sources.title: Mount Laurel Historical Society: villages and suburban growth

communities.title: New Hanover Township
communities.summary: Cookstown gives New Hanover a village center near the North Branch of Crosswicks Creek. Its name recalls William Cooke's mill, while the Godfrey House at the village crossroads and a restored one-room schoolhouse preserve landmarks of the settlement within a township of farmland and Pine Barrens terrain.

communities.title: North Hanover Township
communities.summary: Expanses of farmland and the older crossroads village of Jacobstown give North Hanover a rural center of its own. Jacobstown's older houses and municipal complex form a recognizable settlement within the township, whose agricultural landscape extends north of the military lands associated with McGuire.

sources.title: North Hanover Township Master Plan Reexamination

communities.title: Palmyra Borough
communities.summary: Palmyra sits on the Delaware opposite Philadelphia's Tacony neighborhood, with the Tacony-Palmyra Bridge making that relationship visible across the water. Streets named Market, Arch, Race, and Vine echo Philadelphia, while the borough's own village history grew around the nineteenth-century railroad.

sources.title: Burlington County Hazard Mitigation Plan: Palmyra Profile

communities.title: Pemberton Borough
communities.summary: Pemberton Borough occupies a ridge between the North Branch of Rancocas Creek and Budd Run. Planned as the mill town of New Mills, it retains the narrow lots, workers' houses, and Federal-era homes along streets such as Hanover and Jarvis that reveal how the settlement took shape.

communities.title: Pemberton Township
communities.summary: Pemberton Township combines the lake neighborhoods around Browns Mills with farms and extensive Pinelands woods. At Whitesbog, workers' cottages and a general store preserve an agricultural village where Elizabeth White helped develop the cultivated blueberry, tying a distinctive settlement to the township's cranberry and blueberry-growing history.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Pemberton Township landscape
New Jersey Historic Trust: Whitesbog Village

communities.title: Riverside Township
communities.summary: Riverside's watchcase-factory clock tower remains a recognizable landmark of its industrial past. The town began with Samuel Bechtold's nineteenth-century resort settlement called Progress, then developed a different identity as manufacturing expanded, leaving a history that reaches from a planned retreat to a factory town.

sources.title: Riverside Township Historical Society: Local History

communities.title: Riverton Borough
communities.summary: Riverton's old steamboat landing and Stick-style yacht-club building preserve the riverfront doorway to a town planned as a summer retreat. Architect Samuel Sloan laid out the village and designed its founders' homes in 1851, leaving a planned-settlement history behind the borough's waterfront architecture.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: Riverton Steamboat Landing

communities.title: Shamong Township
communities.summary: Indian Mills and Atsion give Shamong two distinct chapters of Pine Barrens history. Indian Mills recalls the eighteenth-century Brotherton reservation, while Atsion's surviving Greek Revival mansion stands within Wharton State Forest as a reminder of the ironmaking village that developed along the Mullica River.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Cultural Resources
New Jersey DEP: Atsion Mansion History

communities.title: Southampton Township
communities.summary: Vincentown's historic district gives rural Southampton a village center of older homes and civic buildings. Its architecture spans several generations, and the small brick Sally Stretch Keen Memorial Library adds a twentieth-century landmark to a settlement that served the surrounding agricultural community.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: Sally Stretch Keen Memorial Library

communities.title: Springfield Township
communities.summary: Jacksonville, Jobstown, and Juliustown give Springfield its familiar group of three village names. The township lies within northern Burlington County's farm belt, where those older settlements sit in a wider landscape of fields and open land rather than forming a single continuous town center.

communities.title: Tabernacle Township
communities.summary: Tabernacle's place in the Pine Barrens is marked by forest land and the Carranza Memorial. The memorial recalls Mexican aviator Emilio Carranza, whose plane crashed here during a 1928 goodwill flight, adding an international story to the township's wooded Pinelands setting.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission Municipal Fact Book: Tabernacle
New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Carranza Memorial and Place Names

communities.title: Washington Township (Burlington County)
communities.summary: Green Bank and Lower Bank provide village centers within Washington Township's larger Pinelands landscape. Batsto adds a different kind of settlement: an old industrial village whose mansion, mills, store, and workers' cottages preserve the physical form of a community built around ironmaking and later agricultural enterprises.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Pine Barrens Byway Institutional Survey
New Jersey Historic Trust: Batsto Village

communities.title: Westampton Township
communities.summary: Peachfield's country house and the historic settlement of Timbuctoo reveal different chapters of Westampton's past. Peachfield's Colonial Revival appearance comes from a 1929 rebuilding, while Timbuctoo was established in 1826 by free and formerly enslaved Black residents, adding another enduring place name to the township.

communities.title: Willingboro Township
communities.summary: Willingboro's postwar identity grew from Levitt's planned housing community, a major change from the older Quaker township beside Rancocas Creek. The brief Levittown name belonged to that building era before residents restored Willingboro, connecting the new community with a name rooted in its earlier history.

communities.title: Woodland Township
communities.summary: Chatsworth gives Woodland Township a village center amid an extensive Pine Barrens landscape of forest, lakes, and streams. Cranberry bogs and blueberry growing are part of that setting's working history, with local cranberry cultivation reaching back to the nineteenth century.

sources.title: New Jersey Department of Agriculture: Woodland Cranberry Farming

communities.title: Wrightstown Borough
communities.summary: Wrightstown sits beside the military lands of Fort Dix and McGuire, a setting that has shaped its modern identity. The older village became a starting point for Camp Dix's construction in 1917, when Army engineers arrived to establish a training camp for the First World War.

sources.title: Joint Base McGuire-Dix-Lakehurst: Camp Dix History

intro.title: Camden County
intro.summary: Camden County sits directly across the Delaware River from Philadelphia and includes the City of Camden, compact older boroughs, large suburban townships, and more wooded communities toward the east. Its housing stock is equally varied, with rowhouses, early twentieth-century homes, postwar neighborhoods, condominiums, townhouses, and newer subdivisions. PATCO, NJ Transit, I-295, Route 42, Route 30, and the New Jersey Turnpike make transportation a major part of the county's geography. Cooper River Park, the Camden Waterfront, neighborhood downtowns, hospitals, colleges, restaurants, shops, and arts and entertainment venues create distinct local centers throughout the county.

communities.title: Audubon and Audubon Park
communities.summary: Audubon grew from farm tracts and small settlements such as Orston and Cedarcroft into a borough in 1905. Next door, Audubon Park has a different origin: it began as wartime housing for Camden shipyard workers and became a separate borough in 1947, retaining its mutual-housing roots.

communities.title: Barrington
communities.summary: Barrington's beginnings are tied to farms and a railroad stop once called Dentdale. The arrival of rail service encouraged the village that became a borough in 1917; after World War II, former farms and even a local airport gave way to the residential and industrial development that reshaped the town.

communities.title: Bellmawr
communities.summary: Bellmawr's name recalls Ernest C. Bell and the farm he operated, but its local story reaches back to landings and brickmaking along the Timber Creeks. Incorporated in 1926 from Centre Township, the borough also has Revolutionary War connections through Captain William Harrison and the fighting around his Little Timber Creek property.

sources.title: Borough of Bellmawr: History and information

communities.title: Berlin Borough and Berlin Township
communities.summary: The old Long-a-Coming name belongs to Berlin Borough's village history, while Berlin Township remains a separate municipality. In the borough, the nineteenth-century Berlin Hotel became part of the public library after being moved along the White Horse Pike; the township's municipal center is in West Berlin.

sources.title: Marie Fleche Memorial Library: Our history

communities.title: Brooklawn
communities.summary: Brooklawn occupies a Delaware River setting across from Philadelphia, with a residential history tied to South Jersey's shipyards. During World War I, Noreg Village was built here to house workers at shipbuilding facilities in South Gloucester, giving the later borough an origin in the region's wartime industrial expansion.

sources.title: Borough of Brooklawn: 2020 audit community description
National Park Service: Gloucester City Water Works nomination, shipyard housing history

communities.title: Camden City
communities.summary: Camden's Delaware River setting has shaped the city from its early ferry landings to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. Its industrial story includes the Victor Talking Machine Company's recording studios and factories, while the former Cooper's Ferry linked South Jersey with Philadelphia long before a bridge crossed the river.

sources.title: City of Camden: Interactive history mural

communities.title: Cherry Hill
communities.summary: Cherry Hill's neighborhoods grew from the farms and crossroads villages of the former Delaware Township. Places such as Ellisburg and Colestown preserve those older names, while postwar developments including Kingston Estates and Brookfield tell another chapter of the township's transformation; voters adopted the Cherry Hill name in 1961.

sources.title: Cherry Hill Township: Illustrated township history

communities.title: Chesilhurst
communities.summary: Chesilhurst sits entirely within the Pinelands, between Winslow and Waterford Townships. The Camden and Atlantic Railroad's historic corridor passes through the borough, linking its place on today's map with the rail route that connected inland South Jersey communities to Atlantic City in the nineteenth century.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Chesilhurst municipal profile
Bureau of Ocean Energy Management: Camden and Atlantic Railroad historic district assessment

communities.title: Clementon
communities.summary: Clementon Lake and Bottoms Lake are part of a townscape shaped by the north branch of Timber Creek. The downtown grew around the early settlement of Newman's Mills, where dams powered a gristmill and sawmill; Samuel Clement's later land purchase gave the village the name it carries today.

sources.title: Borough of Clementon: The Clementonian, Spring/Summer 2020 history

communities.title: Collingswood
communities.summary: Between Newton Creek and the Cooper River, Collingswood grew from Quaker settlements and family farms into a borough. The Collings-Knight and Thackara houses connect today's town with those early landowners, while the Stokes-Lee property recalls an earlier creekside landing, tavern and nineteenth-century mineral-spring resort.

sources.title: Borough of Collingswood: Historic preservation plan

communities.title: Gibbsboro
communities.summary: Silver Lake sits at the center of Gibbsboro's story, from an early mill settlement to John Lucas's paint-manufacturing town. Lucas bought the mill in 1852, drawn by the water's purity; the borough's historic core still reflects the relationship between the lake, industrial buildings and housing built for owners and workers.

sources.title: Borough of Gibbsboro: Historic preservation element

communities.title: Gloucester City
communities.summary: Gloucester City's western edge follows the Delaware River, where Dutch traders established Fort Nassau in the seventeenth century. Farther inland, the city's designated historic area includes portions of King, Burlington and Willow Streets, preserving a townscape whose history extends well beyond the waterfront and the nearby Walt Whitman Bridge.

sources.title: Gloucester City: Master plan historic preservation element

communities.title: Gloucester Township
communities.summary: Gloucester Township's older settlements left landmarks tucked into today's suburban landscape. In Glendora, the Gabreil Daveis Tavern recalls travelers and watermen moving goods along Timber Creek; in Blenheim, the privately occupied Chew-Powell House and adjoining burial ground preserve another piece of the township's early history.

sources.title: Gloucester Township: Township history and historic sites

communities.title: Haddon Heights
communities.summary: Haddon Heights took shape around an 1890 railroad station and the street grid laid out by the Lippincotts and Charles Hillman. The downtown near the tracks and White Horse Pike, together with early twentieth-century four-square and Colonial Revival houses, still expresses the borough's origins as a planned railroad suburb.

communities.title: Haddon Township
communities.summary: Westmont, Bettlewood, Bluebird and West Collingswood Heights are some of the neighborhood names within Haddon Township. Along Haddon Avenue, buildings stand close to the road on lots laid out before cars became common, preserving the shape of an older business district among the township's residential sections.

sources.title: Haddon Township: Government and neighborhood districts
Haddon Township: Master Plan Reexamination, December 2019

communities.title: Haddonfield
communities.summary: Kings Highway runs through Haddonfield's historic downtown, where the Indian King Tavern connects the borough to the founding of New Jersey. The state legislature met in the tavern during 1777, adopting the Great Seal and changing New Jersey's official designation from colony to state during the Revolutionary War.

sources.title: New Jersey State Park Service: Indian King Tavern

communities.title: Hi-Nella
communities.summary: Hi-Nella fits residential streets and apartment communities into less than a quarter of a square mile. Signey Run marks part of its western landscape, while the Dobbs Farm property is a reminder of the agricultural land that preceded the surrounding suburban development.

sources.title: Borough of Hi-Nella: Municipal stormwater management plan

communities.title: Laurel Springs
communities.summary: Laurel Springs grew beside the Timber Creek mill community known as Laurel Mills, named for the laurel around its lake. A later railroad-era chapter brought Samuel Cord's housing development and stone mansion; the house at Atlantic and Tomlinson Avenues became Borough Hall after the municipality acquired it during the Depression.

sources.title: Borough of Laurel Springs: Early colonial history
Borough of Laurel Springs: Victorian-era history
Borough of Laurel Springs: Cord Mansion history

communities.title: Lawnside
communities.summary: Lawnside's history began as a free African American settlement and continued with its incorporation as a self-governing borough in 1926. The 1845 Peter Mott House gives that story a physical home: the preserved residence is now a museum interpreting Mott's life, the community and its connections to the Underground Railroad.

sources.title: New Jersey Historic Trust: Peter Mott House
New Jersey Historical Commission: Black Heritage Trail

communities.title: Lindenwold
communities.summary: Kirkwood, Lucaston, Laurel Mills and Garden Lake are among the older sections that make up Lindenwold. These earlier settlements retain their own names within the borough, whose German-derived name means 'linden woods' and was chosen by a resident during the community's development.

sources.title: Borough of Lindenwold: Environmental resource inventory history

communities.title: Magnolia
communities.summary: Magnolia's roughly square-mile footprint grew from land held by generations of the Albertson family. That family history remains part of the borough's landscape: engineer John J. Albertson left land opposite Borough Hall for the park bearing his name, linking a present-day gathering place to the town's earlier farms.

communities.title: Merchantville
communities.summary: Merchantville's former train station remains a landmark at the center of town, now used for a café and art activities. Nearby, the old rail corridor has become the Merchantville Mile walking path, threading a borough whose Victorian houses and historic storefronts reflect its nineteenth-century development.

communities.title: Mount Ephraim
communities.summary: The meeting of Kings Highway and the Black Horse Pike is central to Mount Ephraim's story. Ephraim Albertson's Public House stood at that crossroads in the early nineteenth century, and the borough still identifies itself as the 'Village at the Crossroads,' with its municipal offices on the pike.

sources.title: Borough of Mount Ephraim: Community introduction

communities.title: Oaklyn
communities.summary: Newton Lake gives Oaklyn a waterside setting shared with Collingswood and Haddon Township. The borough's neighborhood streets lead toward a small West Clinton Avenue gathering area, where municipal events close several blocks to traffic; the lake and that local center make two distinct focal points within the town.

sources.title: Borough of Oaklyn: Community event notices

communities.title: Pennsauken
communities.summary: Pennsauken has two different river edges: the Delaware waterfront to the west and the Cooper River rowing course to the east. Between them, the township combines residential neighborhoods with a substantial industrial presence, so its identity includes both the river landscape and the workplaces woven into the community.

sources.title: Pennsauken Township: Community overview from EMS

communities.title: Pine Hill (including the former Pine Valley Borough)
communities.summary: Pine Hill takes its name from the pine trees and hills that distinguish its landscape; earlier names included Mount Ararat and Clementon Heights. The nineteenth-century Tomlinson House on Blackwood-Clementon Road is a surviving local landmark, and the borough now includes the former Pine Valley municipality following their 2022 consolidation.

sources.title: New Jersey Government Records Council: Pine Valley consolidation record

communities.title: Runnemede
communities.summary: Timber Creek and its tributaries form Runnemede's western edge, while Irish Hill rises above the lower creek ground. The Black Horse Pike crosses the middle of the borough, but the creekside lake and older residential streets reveal a different side of this early suburban community.

sources.title: Borough of Runnemede: Master plan reexamination

communities.title: Somerdale
communities.summary: Somerdale combines older suburban streets with a newer center built from the former Lion's Head Shopping Plaza. Its redevelopment as CooperTowne brought storefronts designed to resemble smaller main-street buildings, with Gateway Village townhouses connecting the center to surrounding residential streets.

sources.title: Borough of Somerdale: Master Plan Reexamination, June 2017

communities.title: Stratford
communities.summary: Stratford began as an 1880s development named for Stratford-upon-Avon, and its older civic center remains along Union Avenue. The public library there grew from a PTA effort in 1921; nearby, the former Tomlinson mansion on Laurel Road tells a separate story as a home later adapted for institutional uses.

sources.title: Borough of Stratford: Tomlinson mansion and military academy history

communities.title: Tavistock
communities.summary: Tavistock is a small borough adjoining Barrington, Haddonfield and Lawnside, with a landscape closely tied to Tavistock Country Club. Its unusual municipal origin grew from members' wish to play golf on Sundays, and the club remains the borough's polling place as well as a local landmark.

communities.title: Voorhees
communities.summary: Kirkwood Lake and the historic Stafford Farm property show two older layers of Voorhees beneath its suburban development. A former ice company was based at the lake, while the farm's preservation set aside both open land and working acreage, keeping an agricultural thread within the township.

sources.title: Voorhees Township: Stafford Farm preservation history

communities.title: Waterford Township
communities.summary: Waterford Township extends from Atco into a much larger Pinelands landscape, including part of Wharton State Forest. The township lies within the Mullica River basin, with settled areas giving way to woods and stream corridors; its eastern forest lands make it a different setting from Camden County's riverfront suburbs.

sources.title: New Jersey Pinelands Commission: Waterford Township planning profile
New Jersey Forest Service: Waterford Township cedar forest

communities.title: Winslow Township
communities.summary: Winslow covers a broad stretch of Camden County, bringing suburban neighborhoods and older Pinelands villages into one township. Blue Anchor, Elm, Tansboro, Waterford Works and Winslow remain distinct settlements within its Pinelands portion, preserving local village identities across the larger municipality.

sources.title: Winslow Township: 2019 Pinelands master plan reexamination

communities.title: Woodlynne
communities.summary: Woodlynne's small street grid sits beside the North Branch of Newton Creek. At its center, a WPA-era log cabin built for scouting is an unusual landmark in such an urban setting, preserving a piece of the borough's community history within the surrounding residential blocks.

sources.title: Borough of Woodlynne: Stormwater outfall map
National Park Service: Woodlynne Log Cabin nomination

intro.title: Cape May County
intro.summary: Cape May County has 16 municipalities spread across barrier islands, back bays, and the mainland at New Jersey's southern tip. The real estate mix includes Victorian homes, shore cottages, condominiums, duplexes, bayfront and oceanfront properties, and mainland single-family homes on larger lots. Ocean City, the Wildwoods, Sea Isle City, Avalon, Stone Harbor, and Cape May each have distinct resort identities, while Upper, Dennis, Middle, and Lower Townships contain a broader mix of year-round communities and coastal access. The Garden State Parkway, county shore routes, marinas, wildlife refuges, beaches, boardwalks, wineries, and preserved natural areas shape both daily life and the county's strong seasonal rhythm.

sources.title: Cape May County Property Tax Lookup

communities.title: Avalon
communities.summary: Avalon occupies the northern end of Seven Mile Island, with preserved high dunes separating many oceanfront streets from the beach. Street-end walkways pass through that vegetated edge, while fishing boats and marinas give the back-bay side a different relationship to the water.

sources.title: Cape May County: Avalon island setting, dunes and bayfront

communities.title: Cape May
communities.summary: Victorian buildings give Cape May's streets a recognizable architectural character at the southern end of the peninsula. The city's seaside-resort history reaches back to eighteenth-century visitors from Philadelphia, and the National Historic Landmark district preserves the built setting of that long relationship with the shore.

sources.title: City of Cape May: architecture, peninsula setting and resort history

communities.title: Cape May Point
communities.summary: At the cape's tip, Cape May Point sits where the ocean and Delaware Bay meet, on a migration route for birds and butterflies. Founded in 1875, the small community has also been known as Stites Beach and Seagrove.

sources.title: Cape May County: Cape May Point geography, migration and settlement

communities.title: Dennis Township
communities.summary: Dennis Township's identity is spread among villages, including Dennisville, Belleplain, Clermont and South Seaville. In Dennisville, the former 1874 schoolhouse now holds the township museum, while older homes associated with shipbuilders connect the village streets to the area's maritime past.

sources.title: Dennis Township History Museum: township villages and the former schoolhouse
Cape May County: Historic Trail, Dennisville's shipbuilding-era homes

communities.title: Lower Township
communities.summary: The Cape May Canal cuts across Lower Township, dividing a landscape of older settlements and Delaware Bay communities. Town Bank's origins reach back to seventeenth-century whaling, while places such as Cold Spring and Erma reflect the mainland villages that developed before the canal was built during World War II.

sources.title: Lower Township: settlement history and the Cape May Canal

communities.title: Middle Township
communities.summary: Cape May Court House gives Middle Township a county-seat center with older buildings along Main Street. Beyond that center, the township extends through marshes and bayside fishing villages toward Delaware Bay, bringing several distinct mainland communities together within one broad coastal landscape.

sources.title: Cape May County: Middle Township's Main Street, villages and bay landscape
Cape May County: Historic Trail and Cape May Court House

communities.title: North Wildwood
communities.summary: Hereford Inlet and its Victorian lighthouse give North Wildwood's northern waterfront a distinct landmark. The lighthouse dates to 1874, close to the beginnings of Anglesea, the fishing settlement that preceded the present city and connects this end of the island to a working maritime past.

sources.title: Cape May County: North Wildwood, Anglesea and Hereford Inlet Lighthouse

communities.title: Ocean City
communities.summary: Ocean City's street plan grew from a Methodist camp-meeting settlement laid out on Peck's Beach in 1879. The Tabernacle grounds remain a physical link to that founding plan, around which cottages and hotels developed as bridges and the railroad connected the island resort with the mainland.

sources.title: City of Ocean City: Peck's Beach, founding plan and Tabernacle

communities.title: Sea Isle City
communities.summary: Sea Isle City stretches along Ludlam Island, with the oceanfront Promenade forming a long edge to the town. Its resort beginnings grew from Charles Kline Landis's nineteenth-century plans for the island, when canals, cottages and arriving railroads began replacing a largely undeveloped shoreline.

sources.title: Cape May County: Sea Isle City's oceanfront Promenade
Bureau of Ocean Energy Management: Sea Isle City historic development, section 3.3.2.24

communities.title: Stone Harbor
communities.summary: Stone Harbor's built-up island streets sit close to protected coastal habitat. A municipal bird sanctuary occupies land within the town, while Stone Harbor Point opens into beaches and dunes at Hereford Inlet, giving the southern shoreline a different character from the developed blocks farther inland.

sources.title: Cape May County: Stone Harbor's municipal bird sanctuary
Borough of Stone Harbor: Stone Harbor Point conservation area

communities.title: Upper Township
communities.summary: Upper Township brings together a largely rural mainland and the beach community of Strathmere. Older village centers such as Tuckahoe and Petersburg predate the Revolution, giving the township a settlement pattern that reaches from inland crossroads and river communities to the ocean shore.

sources.title: Upper Township: mainland villages and Strathmere history

communities.title: West Cape May
communities.summary: Victorian homes and cultivated land sit close together in West Cape May, where farms remain part of the borough's landscape. Farm markets and the lima bean festival at Wilbraham Park keep its agricultural traditions visible alongside the residential streets.

sources.title: Cape May County: West Cape May's homes, farming and lima bean tradition

communities.title: West Wildwood
communities.summary: Grassy Sound and the Wildwood Canal frame West Wildwood's separate back-bay island. A single bridge connects it with the main Wildwoods island, while a mix of smaller vacation houses and taller replacement homes shows how this waterside borough's residential streets have changed over time.

sources.title: Cape May County: West Wildwood's island, waterways and houses
Cape May County Property Tax Lookup

communities.title: Wildwood
communities.summary: Wildwood's broad beach and Boardwalk give the city a strong oceanfront spine, with amusement piers extending toward the water. The resort's midcentury architecture is visible in its Doo Wop motels, whose neon signs and distinctive forms remain part of the streetscape.

sources.title: Cape May County: Wildwood's Boardwalk, beach and Doo Wop architecture

communities.title: Wildwood Crest
communities.summary: Oceanfront motels and condominiums line Wildwood Crest's beach side, while houses face the back bay. Sunset Lake forms a western waterfront, giving the borough a lakeside shore as well as its broad Atlantic Ocean beach.

sources.title: Cape May County: Wildwood Crest's oceanfront, homes and Sunset Lake

communities.title: Woodbine
communities.summary: Woodbine's rural setting surrounds a town that once served as a busy industrial center. The 1890s Brotherhood Synagogue on Washington Street marks the community's immigrant beginnings, while Woodbine Airport, once a military base, continues in use as a general aviation airfield.

sources.title: Cape May County: Woodbine's rural setting, synagogue and airfield

intro.title: Cumberland County
intro.summary: Cumberland County combines the cities of Bridgeton, Millville, and Vineland with smaller borough, township, agricultural, woodland, river, and Delaware Bay communities. Its housing includes historic downtown properties, ranch and split-level neighborhoods, newer single-family construction, rural homes, farms, and seasonal cottages near the bay. Route 55 is the principal north-south highway, while Routes 47 and 49 connect towns, employment centers, and shore destinations. The Maurice River, preserved forests and wetlands, working farms, Millville's Glasstown Arts District, museums, parks, and wildlife areas give the county a character that is both industrial and rural.

communities.title: Bridgeton
communities.summary: Bridgeton's center straddles the tidal Cohansey River at a crossing that dates to 1716. Its historic streets preserve houses and commercial buildings from an industrial town shaped by glass, metalworking and textiles, with modest paired homes as much a part of the setting as larger Victorian buildings.

sources.title: City of Bridgeton: river crossing, industries and historic buildings

communities.title: Commercial Township
communities.summary: Commercial Township's settlements follow the Maurice River toward Delaware Bay. Port Norris and Bivalve carry the area's oyster-industry history, while Mauricetown's houses on higher ground beside the river recall coastal trade. Laurel Lake began as a twentieth-century summer resort and became a year-round community.

sources.title: Commercial Township: river communities, oyster industry and Laurel Lake

communities.title: Deerfield Township
communities.summary: Rosenhayn and Carmel give Deerfield Township two settlement stories within a landscape of farms, woods and neighborhoods. Rosenhayn was planned after the Civil War using Vineland as a model, while Carmel grew from Beaver Dam, a stopping place on the stagecoach route between Bridgeton and Millville.

sources.title: Cumberland County: Rosenhayn and Carmel settlement history

communities.title: Downe Township
communities.summary: Downe Township's mainland villages lead toward fishing communities on Delaware Bay. Places such as Newport, Dividing Creek and Fortescue give this rural bayshore landscape several centers, with working waterfronts and broad areas of preserved land shaping the township beyond any single village street.

sources.title: Downe Township: bayshore villages and rural landscape

communities.title: Fairfield Township
communities.summary: Open fields, tidal marshes and small settlements shape Fairfield Township between the Cohansey River and Delaware Bay. Fairton's earlier name, New England Town, points to its colonial settlement history, giving one of the township's present village centers a connection to the late seventeenth century.

sources.title: Cumberland County: Fairfield Township municipal profile, landscape and waterways
Cumberland County: Fairton and New England Town history

communities.title: Greenwich Township
communities.summary: Ye Greate Street gives Greenwich its long village spine, following a route laid out in 1684 toward the Cohansey River. Brick farmhouses and the historic district reflect the settlement's years as a working port, while the 1774 tea burning remains part of its Revolutionary history.

sources.title: Greenwich Township: Ye Greate Street, port history and historic buildings

communities.title: Hopewell Township
communities.summary: Hopewell Township's farmland and older villages meet the residential edge of Bridgeton. Roadstown, Bowentown and Old Cohansey remain distinct place names within that rural setting, while housing developments near the city boundary date to the township's growth in the 1950s and 1960s.

sources.title: Hopewell Township: villages and agricultural setting
Hopewell Township: Open Space and Recreation Plan, settlement and residential growth

communities.title: Lawrence Township
communities.summary: Lawrence Township reaches from farmland around Cedarville to tidal marshes and the Delaware Bay shoreline at Bay Point. Those two communities give the township an inland village and a waterfront settlement, with creeks and open agricultural ground forming much of the landscape between them.

sources.title: Lawrence Township: Cedarville, Bay Point and township landscape

communities.title: Maurice River Township
communities.summary: Maurice River Township's history follows a string of river settlements toward Delaware Bay. Port Elizabeth developed as a port, while Dorchester's boatbuilding tradition produced the schooner A. J. Meerwald in 1928; at the river's mouth, East Point Lighthouse marks the meeting of river and bay.

sources.title: Maurice River Township: river villages, shipbuilding and East Point Lighthouse

communities.title: Millville
communities.summary: The Maurice River and Union Lake explain much of Millville's early shape. Waterpower supported the mills from which the settlement grew, while local silica helped glassmaking take hold; the city's later streets developed around a river that linked its industrial center with the wider region.

sources.title: City of Millville: Maurice River, Union Lake and industrial origins

communities.title: Shiloh Borough
communities.summary: Shiloh's village and surrounding farms grew from the early settlement known as Cohansey Corners. Established by Seventh Day Baptist families in the early eighteenth century, the village later straddled Hopewell and Stow Creek townships before becoming a separate borough in 1929.

sources.title: Borough of Shiloh: Cohansey Corners and village history

communities.title: Stow Creek Township
communities.summary: Farms, woodlands and wetlands shape Stow Creek Township in Cumberland County's northwest corner. Along Stow Creek, the village of Jericho grew around grain mills established about 1700, giving the township's rural landscape a history of working waterways as well as cultivated land.

sources.title: Stow Creek Township: rural landscape and location
Cumberland County: Jericho settlement and mill history

communities.title: Upper Deerfield Township
communities.summary: Upper Deerfield's fields and farm-related industries reflect a landscape shaped by agriculture. Around Seabrook, the legacy includes food-processing buildings and a neighborhood of Cape Cod houses associated with Seabrook Farms, connecting the township's rural setting with the twentieth-century development of large-scale farming and frozen foods.

sources.title: Upper Deerfield Township: rural and agricultural setting
Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission: Upper Deerfield Open Space Plan, Seabrook Farms history
Upper Deerfield Township: 2025 Housing Element draft, Seabrook Village built form

communities.title: Vineland
communities.summary: Broad Landis Avenue gives Vineland a physical link to its beginnings as Charles Landis's planned settlement. Laid out around the railroad in the 1860s, the town was intended to serve surrounding farms, and that combination of a defined center and agricultural land remains part of its identity.

sources.title: Cumberland County: Charles Landis and Vineland's original avenue plan
City of Vineland: Landis Avenue and agricultural setting

intro.title: Gloucester County
intro.summary: Gloucester County runs from Delaware River communities through established suburbs and boroughs into farmland and lower-density townships. The county's real estate includes historic homes in Woodbury and older borough centers, postwar neighborhoods, townhouses, newer subdivisions, and properties with larger lots in its southern and eastern sections. I-295, Route 55, Route 42, and the New Jersey Turnpike connect the county with Philadelphia and the rest of South Jersey. Red Bank Battlefield, Scotland Run Park, local downtowns, farm markets, wineries, shopping districts, colleges, and community events reflect the mix of suburban growth and agricultural history found across its 24 municipalities.

communities.title: Clayton
communities.summary: Clayton's identity combines a former glassmaking village with the woods and water around Scotland Run. Once known as Fislertown, the settlement grew around glass factories; the borough's preserved recreational land now includes both local gathering places and the larger natural landscape at its edges.

sources.title: Borough of Clayton: Community background and landscape

communities.title: Deptford Township
communities.summary: Deptford is a collection of neighborhoods with different beginnings, from the former mill settlement of Almonesson to postwar Oak Valley. Lake Almonesson recalls the township's milling and ice-making past, while Oak Valley's Cape Cod, ranch and split-level houses show the later conversion of country-club land into residential streets.

sources.title: Deptford Township: Township history and neighborhoods

communities.title: East Greenwich Township
communities.summary: Mickleton, Clarksboro and Mount Royal are local names within East Greenwich, a township of residential neighborhoods and farmland in western Gloucester County. The municipality was assembled from parts of Greenwich and Mantua, and those smaller communities remain useful landmarks across its wider rural and suburban landscape.

sources.title: State of New Jersey: Local place-name directory

communities.title: Elk Township
communities.summary: Roadside produce stands and working farmland remain part of Elk Township's landscape at Gloucester County's southern end. The Elephant Swamp Trail adds another local landmark, running from the township's recreation complex toward Salem County and reflecting the old rail corridors that once crossed this farming area.

sources.title: New Jersey Department of Transportation: Elephant Swamp trail connection
South Jersey Transportation Planning Organization: South Jersey Trails Design Guide

communities.title: Franklin Township
communities.summary: Franklin Township spreads across a broad, partly forested landscape in southeastern Gloucester County, with farms, lakes and streams draining toward the Maurice River. Franklinville and Malaga belong to its older settlement pattern, while part of the township lies within the Pinelands National Reserve, giving the municipality both village centers and extensive rural land.

sources.title: Franklin Township: History and village development

communities.title: Glassboro
communities.summary: Rowan University's campus and Glassboro's downtown form a present-day center built on older industrial roots. The borough takes its name from glassmaking, and Hollybush Mansion connects those histories: the former Whitney family's home stands on the university campus, where it hosted the Johnson–Kosygin summit in 1967.

sources.title: Borough of Glassboro: History and present-day Glassboro

communities.title: Greenwich Township
communities.summary: Gibbstown is a local community within Greenwich Township, where the C. A. Nothnagle Log House preserves a link to the New Sweden period. The township is one remnant of a much larger early municipality whose former territory became several neighboring Gloucester County towns.

sources.title: Greenwich Township: About the township and Gibbstown
New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency: Gibbstown community landmarks

communities.title: Harrison Township
communities.summary: Historic Main Street in Mullica Hill forms a village center for Harrison Township, with houses ranging from the eighteenth century to the Victorian era. Raccoon Creek helped shape that settlement through milling, while Ewan, Richwood and Jefferson give the wider township several additional community identities.

communities.title: Logan Township
communities.summary: Beckett, Bridgeport, Center Square, Nortonville and Repaupo are the five named areas that make up Logan Township. Their local names continue within a municipality that was originally established as West Woolwich, with Bridgeport holding the town hall and serving as the township's municipal address.

communities.title: Mantua Township
communities.summary: Mantua's original village stands on higher ground overlooking Mantua Creek, the waterway that gave the township its name. Sewell and Barnsboro are other communities within the municipality, while the township's offices remain on Main Street in Mantua, connecting its civic address with the older creekside village.

sources.title: State of New Jersey: Local place-name directory

communities.title: Monroe Township
communities.summary: Williamstown anchors Monroe Township, surrounded by smaller places including Cross Keys, Cecil, Downer and Victory Lakes. Streams such as Four Mile Branch and Scotland Run cross this former 'pine township,' whose village history includes glassmaking and produce canning alongside the earlier use of its forests and sandy ground.

sources.title: Monroe Township: Township and community history

communities.title: National Park
communities.summary: National Park meets the Delaware River at Red Bank Battlefield, where open river views surround the remains of Fort Mercer and the James and Ann Whitall House. The landmark is both a Revolutionary War site and a continuing place for interpreting eighteenth-century life through the house and its gardens.

sources.title: Gloucester County: Red Bank Battlefield Park

communities.title: Newfield
communities.summary: Newfield's streets and older business sites follow the junction where the Atlantic City spur met the main railroad line. The railway brought employees and industry to the village, including a glass factory between the tracks; today's Borough Hall occupies the former First National Bank building.

communities.title: Paulsboro
communities.summary: The Delaware River and Mantua Creek frame Paulsboro's industrial waterfront, while Billingsport preserves the name of an earlier shad-fishing village. The black steel tower of Tinicum Rear Range Lighthouse rises within the borough, continuing a navigation role that began in 1880.

sources.title: Borough of Paulsboro: Tour of Historic Paulsboro

communities.title: Pitman
communities.summary: Pitman Grove gives the borough an unusual center: twelve narrow streets radiate from a tabernacle, surrounded by small cottages with porches and latticework. The pattern began as an 1871 Methodist camp meeting, and the nearby Broadway business district developed as the seasonal settlement became a year-round town.

sources.title: Pitman Historic Preservation Commission: Design Guidelines

communities.title: South Harrison Township
communities.summary: Harrisonville is one local name within South Harrison's agricultural landscape, where the township continues to preserve its farming heritage. Older brick houses remain landmarks along the country roads, including the privately owned Gardiner House, whose gable bears the date 1802 at the Commissioners Road crossroads.

sources.title: State of New Jersey: Locality Search

communities.title: Swedesboro
communities.summary: Swedesboro's center follows Kings Highway south from Raccoon Creek, with a streetscape shaped by its early Swedish and Finnish settlement. The Van Leer/Mortenson Log Cabin now stands beside the Trinity 'Old Swedes' Church cemetery, keeping a surviving early building within the borough's present landscape.

communities.title: Washington Township
communities.summary: Turnersville, Hurffville and Grenloch Terrace are among the local communities that make up Washington Township. At Olde Stone House Village, the George Morgan house shares a site with a rescued post office, church, farmhouse and railroad station, gathering pieces of the area's earlier villages into one physical setting.

sources.title: State of New Jersey: Locality Search
New Jersey Historic Trust: George Morgan Jr. Stone House

communities.title: Wenonah
communities.summary: Wenonah's broad Mantua Avenue and regular blocks reflect a town planned around the West Jersey Railroad in the 1870s. The borough began as farmland redeveloped for a country resort beside Mantua Creek; dams later created recreational lakes, leaving water as well as the street plan central to its identity.

sources.title: Borough of Wenonah: History and Heritage

communities.title: West Deptford Township
communities.summary: West Deptford follows the Delaware River, with local names such as Thorofare and Verga marking communities within the township. At RiverWinds, the riverfront forms a peninsula and cove beside Woodbury Creek, a landscape shaped by decades of dredged material before the township acquired the site.

sources.title: West Deptford Township: RiverCenter Redevelopment Plan, January 2020
City of Woodbury: History and neighboring communities

communities.title: Westville
communities.summary: Big Timber Creek is central to Westville's layout and origins: the old Kings Highway crossed the water here, encouraging a tavern stop and a town. The Thomas West House still stands on River Drive, connecting today's creekside borough to that early crossing community.

communities.title: Woodbury
communities.summary: Woodbury's Main Street district extends from the Woodbury Creek bridge toward the old Mullica Hill and Swedesboro road junction. Gloucester County's seat for more than two centuries, the city also grew around the Green family's nineteenth-century patent-medicine business, giving its center both civic and industrial roots.

communities.title: Woodbury Heights
communities.summary: Glen Lake gives Woodbury Heights a waterside landmark with an industrial beginning: its dam once powered Simon Snook's lumber mill. The surrounding borough grew through planned development on both sides of the railroad, followed by the Southwood and Summit neighborhoods that expanded its residential streets in the twentieth century.

communities.title: Woolwich Township
communities.summary: Preserved farmland forms a continuous stretch around Davidson Road in Woolwich, while tidal Raccoon Creek adds wetlands and meadow to the township's landscape. Lake Narraticon, shared with Swedesboro, gives another waterside setting, linking the surrounding countryside with the neighboring borough.

intro.title: Salem County
intro.summary: Salem County occupies New Jersey's southwestern corner along the Delaware River and Bay, with a landscape of farms, wetlands, creeks, woodland, small boroughs, and the historic City of Salem. Housing ranges from older homes in town centers to farmhouses, modest single-family neighborhoods, and rural properties with more land. Routes 40, 45, and 49 provide the main local connections, with access toward the Delaware Memorial Bridge, Wilmington, Philadelphia, and the rest of South Jersey. Historic sites, wildlife refuges, river and creek access, local farms, Parvin State Park, and preserved open land are central to the county's identity.

communities.title: Alloway Township
communities.summary: Alloway Village and the homes around Alloway Lake form a center within the township's wider rural landscape. Farming shaped much of that countryside, while Wistarburg's glass factory and shipbuilding along Alloway Creek added industries that helped determine where the early community developed.

communities.title: Carneys Point Township
communities.summary: Carneys Point's village history is closely tied to DuPont, whose works grew from a tract on the Delaware River. That industrial connection reached into civic life: the company's former quartermaster building at D and Division Streets later housed the township's offices, courtroom, and police department.

sources.title: Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Industrial History

communities.title: Elmer Borough
communities.summary: Elmer Lake and Muddy Run give Elmer a waterside setting, while an abandoned railroad bed still marks the division between North and South Main Street. The former rail center once drew farmers' wagons to a busy potato market, connecting the borough's village streets with the surrounding agricultural area.

communities.title: Elsinboro Township
communities.summary: Elsinboro combines riverfront homes, agricultural land, and surviving houses from the early eighteenth century. Its Swedish history is remembered at the Fort Elfsborg monument outside the township school, while buildings such as the 1722 Nicholson House preserve another part of the community's early settlement story.

sources.title: Elsinboro Township: Local History and Historic Houses

communities.title: Lower Alloways Creek Township
communities.summary: Hancocks Bridge gives Lower Alloways Creek a historic village at a tidal creek crossing. The Hancock House's patterned brick walls and glazed-brick initials preserve an eighteenth-century landmark beside the old bridge site, where the water and surrounding salt marsh shaped the settlement's setting.

sources.title: National Park Service: Hancock House Historic Nomination
Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Hancocks Bridge

communities.title: Mannington Township
communities.summary: Mannington's farm fields meet the tidal waters and wetlands of Mannington Meadows along the township's western side. The Salem River follows its northern and western boundaries, giving this agricultural community a landscape defined as much by waterways and marsh edges as by cultivated ground.

communities.title: Oldmans Township
communities.summary: Pedricktown and the smaller hamlet of Auburn give Oldmans Township separate village identities within a farming area. Auburn sits on Oldmans Creek, where tugboats once carried local produce toward Philadelphia, linking the older creekside settlement with the agricultural land around it.

sources.title: Salem County Growth Management Plan: Oldmans Settlements
Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Auburn and Pedricktown

communities.title: Penns Grove Borough
communities.summary: Penns Grove's commercial center grew inland from the Delaware riverbank toward Main and Broad streets, the old Dog Town Corner. Helms Cove adds an earlier waterfront chapter: its public landing, ferry, and shipyard served a settlement that later became part of the borough.

sources.title: Penns Grove Borough: Historic Penns Grove
Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Helms Cove

communities.title: Pennsville Township
communities.summary: Pennsville's Delaware River setting carries the history of Swedish settlement near Churchtown and Finnish settlement around Finns Point. Farming and shad fishing once shaped local work, and surviving pre-Revolutionary houses remain within a riverfront community that later developed a substantial industrial chapter.

communities.title: Pilesgrove Township
communities.summary: Pilesgrove's farmland surrounds the separate borough of Woodstown, so the township's countryside stretches around a distinct town center. Within Pilesgrove itself, Sharptown and Yorktown remain older village places among the agricultural lands that extend across the township.

sources.title: Salem County Growth Management Plan: Pilesgrove Villages

communities.title: Pittsgrove Township
communities.summary: Pittsgrove's farming landscape contains distinct older settlements such as Centerton, Olivet, Norma, and Brotmanville. In the southeast, Alliance and its neighboring hamlets preserve the identity of a Jewish agricultural settlement established by immigrants fleeing persecution in Russia, adding a particular settlement story to the township's rural geography.

sources.title: Pittsgrove Township Open Space and Recreation Plan: Local History

communities.title: Quinton Township
communities.summary: Quinton's village history centers on the crossing of Alloway Creek at Quinton's Bridge. The creek also bordered the former glassworks and its workers' housing, where window, coach, and picture glass were made, giving the settlement an industrial history alongside its Revolutionary-era bridge story.

sources.title: Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Quinton and Quinton's Bridge
Salem County Cultural and Heritage Commission: Quinton Glassworks

communities.title: Salem City
communities.summary: Salem's Market Street includes the old county courthouse, whose brick walls and bell tower remain visible links to the eighteenth-century town. Established by Quaker settlers, the city later became a center of glass and bottle manufacturing, adding an industrial history to its older civic streetscape.

sources.title: City of Salem: About Salem City

communities.title: Upper Pittsgrove Township
communities.summary: Upper Pittsgrove's rural landscape is organized around older settlements including Daretown, Monroeville, and Pole Tavern. At Daretown, a lake on the Salem River, its dam, and the old mill give the village a distinct waterside landmark within the township's broader agricultural setting.

sources.title: Salem County Growth Management Plan: Upper Pittsgrove
Upper Pittsgrove Township: Daretown Lake and Mill

communities.title: Woodstown Borough
communities.summary: Memorial Lake occupies the old millpond at the center of Woodstown, connecting the present borough with Benjamin Acton's seventeenth-century gristmill on the Salem River. The historic district also retains the homes of early settler Jechonias Wood and his son, giving the town's namesake a surviving physical presence.

sources.title: Woodstown Borough Newsletter: Brief History of Woodstown
